extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of formal logic and philosophy (logicians, philosophers, advanced philosophy students)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the theory of classification (genus, species, differentia, proprium, accidens) and principles for forming and using classes and general names in logical analysis. Focuses on how names connote attributes, how classes are created, and how classificatory distinctions should be understood and applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: General names connote attributes and create classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Every name the signification of which is constituted by attributes is potentially a name of an indefinite number of objects; by every general name which we introduce, we create a class, if there be any things, real or imaginary, to compose it. In predicating the name we predicate only the attributes; and the fact of belonging to a class does not, in many cases, come into view at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use general names to express connoted attributes; recognize that introducing a general name ordinarily (but not always) produces a class constituted by those attributes. Predication concerns the attributes, not class-membership per se. Examples: God, dragon, mermaid — names may connote attributes even if no real objects correspond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and general language are reciprocally related
rubrics_metrics.description: Classes mostly owe their existence to general language, but sometimes general language owes its existence to classes (e.g., naturalists introduce names for groups for scientific convenience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or constructing classifications, note whether a name was introduced to express an attribute (predication-first) or to bind a convenient class for scientific purposes (classification-first). Treat such names as connotative and analyze their connotation in context; do not assume technical names differ in mode of signification from ordinary connotative names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlimited power to frame classes (division on any attribute)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a fundamental principle in logic that the power of framing classes is unlimited, as long as there is any (even the smallest) difference to found a distinction upon. Take any attribute whatever, and if some things have it and others have not, we may ground on the attribute a division of all things into two classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that any attributable difference can be used to make a class; however, evaluate whether the resulting class is epistemically useful or a 'real Kind' (see below). The mere possibility of forming a class does not make it a significant or natural division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between real Kinds and accidental/artificial classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some classes have properties whose commonality is inexhaustible and indicate a profound, 'real' difference (Kinds); other classes differ only in a finite, determinate way (accidents) and may be merely convenient. Real Kinds are those distinguished by an indeterminate multitude of properties not derivable from one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a classificatory split, ask whether the distinguishing attribute indexes an indeterminate/inexhaustible cluster of further properties (suggesting a real Kind) or whether it is a finite/determinate difference suitable only for practical convenience. Be cautious about labeling classes as 'Kinds' without evidence of such pervasive differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximate (infima) species principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The proximate (or lowest) Kind to which any individual is referable is called its species. When the proximate species is ascertained, the properties common to that species include necessarily the whole of the common properties of every other real Kind to which the individual can be referible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the proximate species to capture the fullest set of common properties for an individual; remember that any larger class including the proximate species will have properties that are a subset of the proximate species' properties. Use proximate species to order genera/species relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five predicables as relations (genus, species, differentia, proprium, accidens)
rubrics_metrics.description: The predicables are a fivefold division of general names based not on differences in meaning but on the kind of class they denote: genus, species, differentia, proprium, accidens. These express the relation the predicate bears to the subject on a particular occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the five labels as relational (context-dependent). A given name can play different predicable roles relative to different subjects (e.g., 'animal' is a genus relative to man, but a species relative to Being). When classifying or analyzing predicates, identify the role by reference to the subject and the classificatory context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus (as a predicable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genus is a class which includes the whole of another class and more; it denotes more than the species and is predicable of a greater number of individuals (e.g., animal is a genus with respect to man).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'genus' to mark broader classes that encompass subordinate species. Note the distinction between popular and technical uses: popular discourse may call many aggregates 'genus' that Aristotelian logic would exclude if not of the 'essence' (i.e., a real Kind). When structuring hierarchies, ensure genus genuinely includes subordinate species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species (as a predicable / proximate species)
rubrics_metrics.description: A species is the proximate Kind to which individuals are referred; it must connote more than the genus (a surplus of connotation) and, when infima, cannot be further divided into Kinds without ceasing to be the proximate species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define species by the additional connotation beyond the genus (the differentia). Check whether further subdivisions would produce true Kinds; if not, treat those subdivisions as accidental or merely classifying conveniences rather than species in the rigorous sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentia (specific difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Differentia is that surplus of connotation which must be added to the connotation of the genus to complete the connotation of the species; it distinguishes a given species from all other species of the same genus. The differentia may vary according to the principle and purpose of the classification and may be ordinary or a special/technical connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the differentia as the distinguishing component of meaning beyond the genus; be aware it can be chosen for practical or scientific purposes (e.g., naturalists may make differentia 'four incisors...' for their taxonomy). When defining terms, state whether the differentia is technical or ordinary and justify the selection by classificatory aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proprium (property distinct from connotation but necessarily following)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Proprium is an attribute which belongs to all individuals in the species and, though not connoted by the specific name, follows necessarily from some connoted attribute. There are two kinds: (1) follows by demonstration (logical consequence), (2) follows by causation (causal consequence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing properties as 'propria', show how they follow necessarily from the connoted attributes — either by demonstrative proof (e.g., geometric consequences) or by causal inference (e.g., capacities that follow from a connoted power). Distinguish propria from differentia (not part of the connotation) and from accidents (not necessary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidens (accident): separable and inseparable
rubrics_metrics.description: Accidens includes attributes neither involved in the signification of the name nor known to have any necessary connection with connoted attributes. They are divided into inseparable accidents (universal in experience but not necessary — e.g., blackness of known crows) and separable accidents (not universal or not constant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify observed attributes as accidental when there is no known necessary link to the species' connotation. Further distinguish whether an accident is inseparable (empirically universal but not logically necessary) or separable (variable among individuals or times). Use these distinctions to avoid conflating empirical universalities with logical necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotation (not 'essence') as the ground for Differentia/Proprium/Accidens distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between Differentia, Proprium, and Accidens is not grounded in the nature of things but in the connotation of names; the schoolmen's talk of 'essence' merely reflects which properties are connoted by a name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing classificatory language, focus on what a name connotes (ordinary or technical meaning) rather than on metaphysical claims of 'essence'. Resist treating 'essence' as an objective metaphysical ground distinct from linguistic connotation; instead, explicate which properties are included in the term's connotation and how further properties follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility and purpose-dependence of classificatory demarcations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical convenience justifies making main demarcations in arrangements of objects run along lines not coinciding with any distinction of Kind. Where genera and species are real, it is permissible to mark distinctions by those properties which considerations of practical convenience most strongly recommend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow classifiers (especially scientists) latitude to define terms of art or to impose special connotations to serve investigative or practical ends. When judging a classification, evaluate whether the demarcation serves its intended purpose and whether technical connotations are made explicit to avoid ambiguity.
